Supersede

soo-per-SEED -- from Latin super- ('above') + sedere ('to sit'); literally 'to sit above/in place of.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To supersede is to replace something, especially something older or outdated, by taking its place.

The museum's newly translated placards will supersede the decades-old English-only descriptions visitors had relied on for years.

Worked Example

The library's new digital catalog superseded the old card-catalog drawers almost overnight.

The digital catalog didn't just exist alongside the old one -- it fully took its place, which is what it means for something to supersede another.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

replace: Replace is the everyday word for putting one thing where another was — you replace a battery, a tire, a broken window. Supersede is formal and one-directional: something newer or higher takes over, and the old version is left outdated.

override: To override is to prevail over something without removing it: the rule that is overridden stays on the books and simply loses whenever the two conflict. When a new rule is meant to supersede another, the old version is genuinely retired and its place is taken.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something in its original state

retain: to continue to have or use something

Where it sits · how forceful the takeover is — displace → supersede → supplant

displace vs. supersede: Displace is weaker than supersede: to displace an old filing routine is to nudge it out of everyday use, while to supersede it is to push it aside completely and take its place for good.

supplant vs. supersede: Supplant is stronger than supersede: a new policy simply supersedes an outdated one, but a deputy who supplants his own mentor has gone further, seizing the position itself through quiet, forceful ambition.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — super-

prefix — super-: above, over (Latin)

root — sede

root — sede: to sit (Latin (sedere))

Put it together

Put it together: Supersede combines Latin super- ('above, over') with sedere ('to sit') -- whatever supersedes another thing has taken the seat above it, literally sitting in its place.

Use the root in a new word: session

Use the root in a new word: session: A session -- a sitting, such as a court session -- comes from that same Latin root, sedere.

Root Check

Word Choice

Supersede is most natural for rules, versions, technologies, or job titles -- things that get formally replaced by a newer or higher version -- rather than for casual, everyday substitutions.
